sections.what:
What is a programming language?

A formal system for expressing algorithms, data manipulation, rules and interactions with computers. Code follows the language's syntax (how valid code is written) and semantics (what it means). A compiler, interpreter, virtual machine, runtime, or a mix of these then executes or translates it into operations the computer can perform.

Career lensLanguages are the most visible skill on a CV, but employers hire for the fundamentals a language carries: problem decomposition, debugging discipline, testing and system thinking. Treat a language as a vehicle for fundamentals.

sections.exec:
How code gets executed

Ahead-of-time compilation

Compiled to native machine code before it runs.

C · C++ · Go · Rust

Bytecode + virtual machine

Compiled to an intermediate form, executed by a runtime.

Java → JVM bytecode · C# → .NET IL

Interpreted / runtime

Executed by a language runtime; modern ones also use JIT compilation.

Python · JavaScript

Transpilation

One source language transformed into another before execution.

TypeScript → JavaScript

Keep in mind: "compiled" and "interpreted" are simplified labels. Modern runtimes combine parsing, bytecode, JIT compilation, caching, optimisation and native execution.

Deep dive: what happens when you "run" Python or JavaScript Mid

  1. Lexing/parsing: source text is tokenised and parsed into an abstract syntax tree (AST).
  2. Lowering: the AST becomes bytecode (CPython .pyc; V8 Ignition bytecode).
  3. Execution + profiling: the interpreter runs bytecode and records type/branch profiles of hot paths.
  4. JIT optimisation: hot functions are recompiled to machine code (V8 TurboFan, PyPy tracing JIT). Broken assumptions trigger a deopt back to the interpreter.
  5. Runtime services: garbage collection, built-ins and FFI boundaries run alongside your code.

Consequences: the first run of Python code is slower than the second (bytecode caching); micro-benchmarks can lie (JIT warm-up); a deopt explains why a function suddenly slows down after a type change.

sections.concepts:
Core concepts that transfer

ConceptWhy it matters

Deep dive: type systems, the most transferable concept

AxisMeaningExamples
  • Gradual typing is the industry's compromise: Python typing (mypy/pyright) and TypeScript add static guarantees without losing dynamic flexibility.
  • Generics let code work over many types safely; understanding variance (in/out, covariance/contravariance) is a real mid-level discriminator.
  • Sum types / pattern matching (Rust enum + match, sealed classes in Java/Kotlin, TS discriminated unions) make invalid states unrepresentable.
  • Testing types: in static languages the compiler is a free, fast test suite; dynamic languages need more tests to cover what a compiler would catch.

sections.sql:
SQL & database programming

SQL (Structured Query Language) is generally considered a programming language, more specifically a domain-specific language (DSL) for querying and managing relational databases. It is declarative: developers describe the desired data operation or result, while the database management system determines how to execute it. SQL complements general-purpose languages such as Python, Java, C#, JavaScript, Go and Rust.

Declarative vs. imperativeIn Python you write the loop that walks through customers and keeps the German ones. In SQL you write SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'DE', and the database's query planner chooses whether to scan the table or use an index. Most applications use both: a general-purpose language for logic, SQL for the data.

sections.ai:
AI-assisted development

AI coding assistants are standard: 82% of developers in Stack Overflow's 2025 survey used OpenAI's GPT models for development in the past year. That changes what to learn.

Fundamentals matter more

Assistants accelerate people who can review, correct and verify code, and amplify gaps for those who can't.

Verification is the career

Describe requirements precisely (inputs, outputs, edge cases, constraints), then test the result like code you didn't write.

Know what you ship

You own licence, security and correctness. Never paste secrets into assistants; scan generated dependencies.

Language synergy

Help is strongest in mainstream languages (Python, TypeScript, Java) and weaker in niche languages and internal frameworks.

Still differentiating: problem decomposition, architecture, debugging production systems and judgement about tradeoffs.

sections.qa:
From a QA perspective

A QA engineer doesn't need to become a full-time developer. Programming literacy improves test design, automation, API testing, debugging, log analysis, CI/CD work and communication with developers.

    ISTQB and programming languagesISTQB certifications are tool- and language-agnostic: they do not teach or require proficiency in any specific programming language. ISTQB focuses strictly on software testing methodologies, principles, terminology and frameworks. The programming skills on this page complement a certification; they are not part of it.
sections.path:
Structured learning path

Five phases from first program to mid-level engineer. Each phase has a goal, what to learn, what to build, and "done when" criteria. Move on when you meet the criteria, not when the calendar says so.

How to use this pathTimings assume about 10–15 hours a week; full-time learners can often halve them. Stay with one main language until phase 3. Spend most of your time building and debugging, not watching tutorials. After each phase, retake the related quizzes and clear your review list.

Where the rest of the hub fits: the numbered steps are in the learning sequence below, the stage checklists (internship, junior, mid-level) measure readiness, the project table gives a build for each level, and the SQL progression runs alongside phases 2–5.

selfCheck: Can you explain the difference between a language, runtime, library and framework?
Language = rules; runtime = executes it; library = code you call; framework = calls your code.
Can you run code from both an IDE and a terminal?
Know the exact command your IDE runs for you (python app.py, npm test, dotnet run).
Can you interpret a compiler/interpreter/runtime error?
Read the error type, the message, then the first stack frame in your own code.
Can you write a small function and test normal, boundary and invalid inputs?
For age 18–65: test 30, then 17/18/65/66, then -1, null and "abc".
Can you trace data through modules and identify side effects?
Follow one value from input to output; note every write to a file, DB, network or shared state.
Can you explain where dependencies come from and how versions are controlled?
Registry (npm, PyPI, Maven Central), manifest, lock file, semantic versioning.
Can you reproduce a defect before attempting a fix?
A fix you can't verify against a reproduction is a guess.
Can you explain what your tests prove, and what they do not?
Tests show the presence of defects, not their absence (ISTQB principle 1).
Can you name a performance, reliability and security risk in a small app?
E.g. N+1 queries, no retries/timeouts on HTTP calls, unvalidated input reaching SQL.
Can you review AI-generated code and explain why it is (or is not) correct and safe?
Check edge cases, error paths, invented APIs, licence and new dependencies, then run the tests.

sqlSkills: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
The four CRUD statements: read, create, change and remove rows.
WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT/OFFSET
Filter rows, sort results and page through them.
JOINs
Combine tables: INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps every row from the left table; RIGHT, FULL and CROSS joins where the dialect supports them.
Aggregation
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX with GROUP BY; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, WHERE filters rows before it.
Subqueries and CTEs
Queries inside queries; WITH (common table expressions) names each step so complex queries stay readable.
Schema and constraints
Tables, rows and columns; primary keys identify rows, foreign keys link tables; NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK protect data.
Transactions and ACID
BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK group changes so they all apply or none do: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
Indexes and query plans
Indexes speed up lookups at a write cost; EXPLAIN shows how the database will run a query.
SQL injection prevention
Never build SQL from user input by string concatenation; use parameterised queries or prepared statements.
Migrations and test data
Versioned schema changes (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, EF Core, Prisma), seed data and repeatable test datasets.
Dialect differences
PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server/T-SQL, Oracle and SQLite share a core but differ in syntax and features.
dialects: Standards-focused and feature-rich: JSONB, arrays, powerful indexing. A common default for new projects.
LIMIT n OFFSET m or LIMIT m, n
Very widely deployed in web stacks. InnoDB is the transactional engine; identifiers are quoted with backticks.
TOP n or OFFSET m ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY
Microsoft ecosystem and .NET. T-SQL adds procedural extensions; identifiers are quoted with square brackets.
Enterprise and finance. PL/SQL for procedural code; an empty string is treated as NULL.

sqlExamples.code:
SELECT name, country
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'DE'
ORDER BY name
LIMIT 10;
sqlExamples.note: You describe the result (German customers, alphabetically, first 10); the database decides how to find them.

sqlExamples.code:
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(o.id)             AS order_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) >= 2
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
sqlExamples.note: LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no orders, and COUNT(o.id) counts only matched orders. HAVING then keeps customers with at least two orders.

sqlExamples.code:
WITH spend AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, s.spent
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
WHERE s.spent > (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM spend)
ORDER BY s.spent DESC;
sqlExamples.note: The CTE names an intermediate result so each step reads top to bottom. The subquery compares every customer with the average.
Atomicity in practice: a transfer must never debit one account without crediting the other.
Before the index, expect a sequential scan of the whole table; after it, an index scan. Indexes speed up reads but add cost to every write.

sqlExamples.code:
# UNSAFE: user input becomes part of the SQL text (SQL injection)
# cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = '{name}'")

# SAFE: the driver sends the value separately from the SQL
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = %s", (name,))
row = cur.fetchone()
sqlExamples.note: Placeholder syntax varies by driver (%s in psycopg and mysql-connector, ? in sqlite3 and JDBC, @name in ADO.NET), but the rule is the same: never concatenate input into SQL.

snippets.note: Python and C# read almost like a sentence. Go deliberately has no built-in filter/map, so a plain loop is idiomatic. Rust's iterator chain compiles down to the same machine code as the loop.

code.Python:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
total = sum(n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0)
print(total)  # 12

snippets.note: Two error models: Python, TypeScript, Java and C# throw exceptions; Go returns an error value next to the result and Rust returns a Result the caller must handle. Boundary tests for all six: 17, 18, 65, 66 and -1.

snippets.task: Read a file and handle errors
snippets.note: Catch the specific error you expect (file not found) and let everything else surface. Java makes you declare checked exceptions (throws IOException); in Go and Rust the error is a value you have to look at, and Rust's match won't compile until every case is handled.

Same goal, three models: async/await on an event loop (Python, TypeScript, C#), threads (Java virtual threads, Rust scoped threads) and goroutines (Go). Both tasks wait at the same time, so the total is about 1 second, not 2.

code.Python:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name: str, seconds: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)  # stands in for a network call
    return f"{name} done"

async def main() -> None:
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("users", 1), fetch("orders", 1))
    print(results)  # ~1 s total, not 2

asyncio.run(main())
